summary:
Workplace Insight reports on new research suggesting that the way people move may offer clues about mental health symptoms and behaviour patterns. Researchers from Northwestern University in Illinois and other institutions examined relationships between movement characteristics and psychological symptoms including anxiety, depression, mania, dissociation, substance use and psychosis. Movement difficulties had previously been linked to schizophrenia and other disorders, but it was unclear whether specific movement types map to specific symptoms rather than to diagnostic categories.

The study analysed data from 3,460 participants in the Multi-Site Assessment of Psychosis-Risk study. Participants self-reported psychological symptoms plus movement and physical activity information, including coordination problems and involuntary movements. Overall movement problems, involuntary or uncontrolled movements and coordination difficulties were positively associated, to varying degrees, with all psychological symptom domains examined. Greater physical activity was associated with mania and substance use symptoms, while lower activity levels were associated with detachment, fear and distress. No simple one-to-one connections between individual movement patterns and particular symptoms were found.

The piece stresses that for employers and occupational health professionals this is not evidence that workplace behaviour or movement should be used to identify or diagnose an employee's mental health. Measures were self-reported and the study does not establish movements as reliable indicators of specific conditions. Instead, motor characteristics could add a dimension for researchers and clinicians studying mechanisms, prognosis and treatment of serious mental illness, functioning as a broad marker and sometimes a more specific predictor.

The work supports a transdiagnostic approach, using the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP), which organises psychological problems by overlapping dimensions rather than discrete categories. The authors call for further research including people with diagnosed mental illnesses. The paper, by Jessica Fattal and colleagues, appeared online in Clinical Psychological Science on 15 June 2026.
